sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Independently read the actual CREATE EXTERNAL MODEL (Transact-SQL) receipt, especially owner_name and both Permissions subsections. The creation/altering subsection documents database-level CREATE EXTERNAL MODEL or ALTER ANY EXTERNAL MODEL permissions and shows GRANT statements. The separate External model grants subsection says a principal using a model in an AI function must be granted EXECUTE, and shows GRANT EXECUTE ON EXTERNAL MODEL::MODEL_NAME TO [<PRINCIPAL>]. owner_name also explains why existing ownership can affect explicit access requirements. These are permission grants, not execution of CREATE, ALTER or inference. The candidate excludes owner/administrator bypasses and prohibits model-management authority, leaving the exact named-model EXECUTE grant. The reference applies to Azure SQL Database; the local ONNX Preview example does not change this remote object-permission distinction.

Independently read Create and manage external models in SQL. The Important paragraph in Use external models with AI functions expressly instructs GRANT EXECUTE ANY EXTERNAL ENDPOINT TO [user_or_role] for endpoint callers. Other sections distinguish stored model metadata, inference and database-object management. This supports a separate outbound-endpoint permission; it does not claim that endpoint authorization grants EXECUTE on every external model. The stem states that endpoint permission, authentication, model configuration and input access already exist. Its missing authorization is therefore derived from the product reference's named-model grant rather than the training sample's abbreviated provisioning sequence.

choiceReviews.rationale: Read literally as an additional permission grant, CREATE EXTERNAL MODEL gives database model-creation authority. That violates the explicit invocation-only requirement even before considering any subsequent DDL; it is not the narrow EXECUTE grant on SupportEmbedding. Literal positive countercontext: a deployment principal is responsible for registering external model definitions and needs the documented database CREATE EXTERNAL MODEL permission. Granting this exact permission is then appropriate; the reference shows that GRANT in its creation/altering subsection. I do not claim that the grant itself creates a model, that it is syntactically invalid, or that a recipient could never invoke any model it separately owns or is authorized to use.

The product reference explicitly requires EXECUTE on an external model to use it in an AI function and supplies the EXTERNAL MODEL::object grant grammar. Substituting the existing identifier SupportEmbedding yields the named permission in this option. Literal confirming context is the given non-owner application principal: input reads, external-endpoint invocation and configured authentication are already available, and it needs usage of this one model without management authority. GRANT EXECUTE ON EXTERNAL MODEL::SupportEmbedding TO [the_application_principal] supplies that documented object capability. This is an authorization statement, not an inference call, and the endpoint permission remains a separate prerequisite.

ALTER ANY EXTERNAL MODEL is a database-wide model-management permission, directly documented in the creation/altering subsection. It exceeds the stem's prohibition on creating or altering definitions and is not the requested object-limited invocation grant. Literal positive countercontext: a deployment-maintenance role is authorized to manage external model definitions across the database and needs the ALTER ANY EXTERNAL MODEL grant shown in the reference. Granting that permission, as written, is suitable for that role; actually altering a model would be a later operation. Rejection here is based on excessive management authority, not an unsupported assertion about every permission implication or ownership case.

The application already has EXECUTE ANY EXTERNAL ENDPOINT. Reissuing that same grant does not supply the distinct model EXECUTE permission required by the product reference. Literal positive countercontext preserving 'again': an application's previously provisioned endpoint permission is no longer present after reprovisioning, while its named-model EXECUTE permission is already in place. Granting EXECUTE ANY EXTERNAL ENDPOINT at database scope again restores the missing endpoint authorization described by the training unit's explicit GRANT instruction. That hypothetical changes which entitlement is missing, not what the grant does. It is not the stated situation, in which the endpoint entitlement is already present and the model entitlement is absent.
